Memorandum
released August 28, 2009. Original judgment has been corrected, with text of
memorandum appended.

IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

BC Securities Commission v.
Hrappstead,

2009 BCSC 1162

Date: 20090827

Docket:
S091867

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

British Columbia Securities Commission

Plaintiff

And

Kenneth Walter Hrappstead,

Kenneth Walter Hrappstead doing business as North American Group

and the said North American Group

Defendants

And

British Columbia Securities
Commission,

Acting Executive Director of B.C. Securities Commission, Michael J. Watson,

British Columbia Ministry of Finance, Minister Colin Hansen,

Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
British Columbia Royal Canadian Mounted Police “E” Division, Vancouver
Commercial Crime Section,

Market Group, Ministry of Public Safety, Minister Peter Van Loan,

Brent W. Aitkens, Roy Wares, Diane K. Wolch, Patricia A.A. Taylor,

Elizabeth J. O’Hea, Cst. Lai-Shan Ng. Corporal George F. Pemberton,

George L. Reid,

Defendants by Counterclaim

Before:  The Honourable Madam Justice Gropper

Corrected Judgment:  The Supreme Court file number and the Judgment
date were corrected on August 28, 2009

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for Plaintiff, B.C. Securities
Commission and counsel for the defendants by counterclaim: Acting Executive
Director Michael J. Watson, Roy Wares, Diane Wolch, Patricia Taylor and
Elizabeth O’Hea:

W.L. Roberts

For the Defendant:  K.W. Hrappstead:

Counsel for the Defendants by
Counterclaim: R.C.M.P., B.C. R.C.M.P. “E” Division, Vancouver Commercial
Crime Section Market Group, Cst. Ng, Cpl. Pemberton and George Reid and
Minister Van Loan (The Federal Defendants by Counterclaim):

British Columbia Ministry of Finance, and
Minister Colin Hansen (The Provincial Defendants by Counterclaim):

In Person

J. Mules

T. Callan

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

August 6, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

August 27, 2009

Introduction

[
1
]

This is an application by the BC Securities
Commission (the “Commission”) for judgment against the defendant, Kenneth
Walter Hrappstead under RR. 18 and 18A.  It is also an application by all the
defendants by counterclaim (some are entities, which cannot be sued) to strike
the defendant’s statement of defence and counterclaim under R. 19(24).

Issues

[
2
]

There are two issues:

1.         Is the Commission entitled to
summary judgment in accordance with R. 18 or R. 18A?

2.         Should Mr. Hrappstead’s
statement of defence and counterclaim be struck in accordance with R. 19(24)?

Background

[
3
]

The Commission issued a decision (the
“decision”) against Mr. Hrappstead, and Mr. Hrappstead doing business as North
American Group on April 7, 1999.  It imposed an administrative penalty on Mr.
Hrappstead of $1,500 (the “fine”), after finding that Mr. Hrappstead was
trading in securities without registration and acted as an advisor without
registration, contrary to s. 34 of the
Securities Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c.
148
(the “
Act
”).

[
4
]

Section 163(1) of the
Act
allows the
Commission to file its decision at any time in a Supreme Court Registry by
filing a copy of the decision certified by the chair of the Commission.
Section 163(2) provides that once filed in the Supreme Court Registry, “...a
decision of the commission has the same force and effect, and all proceedings
may be taken on it, as if it were a judgment of the Supreme Court.”

[
5
]

Mr. Hrappstead did not appeal the decision of
the Commission.  The process for reviews and appeals is outlined in s. 167 of
the
Act
.  An appeal of a decision is to the Court of Appeal with leave
of a justice of that court.

[
6
]

Mr. Hrappstead has not satisfied the judgment by
paying the amount owed.

[
7
]

In March 2009, the Commission filed a writ of
summons and statement of claim to renew the judgment.  When the writ and
statement of claim were served on Mr. Hrappstead, he filed his statement of
defence and counterclaim.

The Decision of the Commission

[
8
]

The decision refers to the background that gave
rise to the hearing.  The staff of the Commission alleged that:

(a) Hrappstead
doing business as North American Group, held information sessions with
investors encouraging them to invest in ‘High Yield Investment Programs’ which
promised to pay up to 2100% return with no risk;

(b) the
Investment Programs constituted a “security” for which no prospectus was issued
and no exemption was available, contrary to s. 61 of the
Act
; and

(c) by
soliciting investments in the Investment Programs, Hrappstead traded in
securities and acted as an advisor without registration, contrary to s. 34 of
the
Act
.

[
9
]

The Commission noted that the R.C.M.P. received
information in April 1997, that Mr. Hrappstead was operating an investment
program.  Cpl. George Pemberton undertook an investigation.  Cst. Lai-Shan Ng
acted undercover as a potential investor and approached Mr. Hrappstead in May
1997.  From May to July 1997, Cst. Ng had several conversations with Mr.
Hrappstead.  She was provided with information regarding the investment
programs.

[
10
]

Mr. Hrappstead told Cst. Ng that he introduced
people to the investment programs and that he had identified and recommended
good investments.  He had two investment programs available.  A minimum
investment of $300,000 US would yield $1 million US in four months.  The second
investment for $125,000 US would yield $600,000 US in one month.

[
11
]

Cst. Ng requested written materials, which Mr.
Hrappstead provided to her.  The materials disclosed that Mr. Hrappstead would
be entitled to 50% of the profits earned by the proposed investors.  When Mr.
Hrappstead learned that the R.C.M.P. was investigating him and he was told that
he would be arrested, Mr. Hrappstead ceased his operation and cooperated
completely with the Commission.  He denied he did anything wrong.

[
12
]

Mr. Hrappstead did not attend the hearing before
the Commission.  He provided an affidavit for the Commission’s consideration.
The Commission considered the affidavit, but declined to give it weight as it
contradicted the
viva voce
evidence that was produced in the hearing.

[
13
]

The Commission did not find that Mr. Hrappstead
sold any of the investment programs, although he had prepared and disseminated
the materials describing them; prepared the forms of agreement for signatures
by investors; conducted information sessions with groups of investors; and had
met with individual investors.  The Commission deduced that “[a]ll of these
activities would be meaningless if the intent were not to further the
participation by investors in the Investment Programs.”

[
14
]

The Commission concluded that Mr. Hrappstead
traded in securities without registration and acted as an advisor without
registration, contrary to s. 34 of the
Act
.  It ordered, among other
things, that Mr. Hrappstead pay an administrative penalty of $1,500, in
accordance with s. 162 of the
Act
.

Statement of Defence and Counterclaim

[
15
]

Mr. Hrappstead denies the claims in the
Commission’s statement of claim and makes the following claims and allegations
in his counterclaim:

a.         “the
defendant” misrepresented facts at the hearing;

b.         the
respondent was falsely accused by “the defendant”;

c.         “the defendant”
failed to apply discretion in a fair and equitable             manner;

d.         “the defendant”
failed to consider the respondents’ affidavit       evidence at the hearing;
and

e.         “the defendant”,
specifically the “R.C.M.P.” and Constable Ng   provided false information to
the hearing

(collectively, the “evidence
claims”).

[
16
]

Mr. Hrappstead made the following claims and
allegations relating to the
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
:

a.         “the defendant” through the
Commission staff and R.C.M.P.,      failed to provide the respondent with
written statements that     demonstrate the respondent’s
Charter
rights
will be protected;       and

b.         “the defendant” has
circumvented the respondent’s
Charter
rights

(collectively, the “
Charter

Claims”).

[
17
]

Mr. Hrappstead makes the following claims and
allegations related to the Commission’s alleged distribution to the media of
information pertaining to the defendant:

a.         “the defendant”,
specifically Michael J. Watson, failed to use his           discretion to
expunge Mr. Hrappstead’s records; and

b.         “the defendant”,
specifically the Commission staff, published     false and misleading
information about Mr. Hrappstead through            the media

(collectively, the “defamation claims”).

[
18
]

Mr. Hrappstead makes the following claims and
allegations relating to the R.C.M.P. investigative techniques:

a.         “the defendant”,
specifically the R.C.M.P., libelled the respondent by relying on the notes taken
by Cst. Ng in the course of the R.C.M.P. investigation into the defendant’s
activities;

b.         “the defendant”,
specifically the R.C.M.P., was biased in relying on the notes taken by Cst. Ng
in the course of the R.C.M.P. investigation into the defendant’s activities;
and

c.         “the defendant”,
specifically Cst. Ng, entrapped the defendant during the course of the R.C.M.P.
investigation

(collectively “the investigation claims”).

[
19
]

Mr. Hrappstead alleges that “the defendant”,
specifically the R.C.M.P. and the staff of the Commission, committed fraud by
misrepresenting facts (the “fraud claim”).

[
20
]

Mr. Hampstead’s references to the “defendants”
are reference to the defendants by counterclaim.  His reference to a particular
“defendant” is to a defendant by counterclaim.

Is the Commission entitled to judgment?

Position of the Parties

[
21
]

The decision was rendered on April 7, 1999.  At
that time, the
Court of Appeal Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 77, provided that
the limitation period for filing a leave to appeal expired after 30 days, that
is, on May 7, 1999.  The Commission points out that Mr. Hrappstead did not
appeal the decision before May 7, 1999, nor has he filed for an extension of
time to apply for leave to appeal.  There is no basis upon which Mr. Hrappstead
may now challenge the decision.  He remains liable to the Commission in the
amount of $1,500 plus interest.

[
22
]

Mr. Hrappstead asserts that he was not selling
securities without a license; he did not have securities to sell.  He asked the
Executive Director to protect his rights.

[
23
]

Mr. Hrappstead filed an affidavit for the
Commission to consider in its hearing on January 26, 1999, as he had no
financial resources to attend.  He says that the Commission failed to allow the
affidavit.

[
24
]

While Mr. Hrappstead received the decision of
the Commission, he says that he had no money to commence an appeal.  He thought
it was an invoice.  Mr. Hrappstead was not aware that a judgment had been filed
and he received no other information in regard to it until the Commission filed
its writ of summons and statement of claim to renew the judgment.

[
25
]

Mr. Hrappstead is concerned that none of the
defendants by counterclaim, including members of the Commission, had taken an
oath of office, which is required for public servants.  He also claims that he
did not receive a fair and impartial hearing from the Commission.

Decision

[
26
]

At the time of the decision, April 7, 1999, s.
167 of the
Act
set out the procedure for appealing a decision of the
Commission:

167 (1) A person directly affected by a
decision of the commission ...

may appeal to
the Court of Appeal with leave of a justice of that court.

[
27
]

As of April 7, 1999, s. 14 of the
Court of
Appeal Act
read, in part:

14        (1)        The time limit for bringing an
appeal or an application                       for leave to appeal is

(a)        30 days, commencing on the day
after the order       appealed from is pronounced, or

(b)        if
another enactment specifies a different period, that           different
period.

(2)        An
appeal or application for leave to appeal is brought

(a)        by
filing a notice of appeal or notice of an application            for leave to
appeal in a registry, and

(b)        by
serving a copy of the notice on every respondent,            unless a justice
orders that service on a respondent   may be dispensed with.

[
28
]

Mr. Hrappstead agrees that he did not file an
application for leave to appeal nor has he filed an application for an
extension of time to file an application for leave to appeal.  He has not
appealed the decision.  Mr. Hrappstead’s complaints and concerns about the
Commission and its decision are properly the subject of an appeal.  This court
does not have the jurisdiction to entertain an appeal from the Commission.

[
29
]

Mr. Hrappstead has no basis to challenge the
decision that requires him to pay $1,500 to the Commission, plus interest.
Judgment is therefore granted to the Commission in the amount of $1,500 plus
interest.

Should
Mr. Hrappstead’s statement of claim and counterclaim be struck?

Position of the Parties

[
30
]

The Commission says that Mr. Hrappstead’s
allegations all relate to conduct that the Commission did in furtherance of
their duties.  There is no allegation regarding the Commission’s conduct
outside of their duties, nor is bad faith alleged.  In essence, Mr. Hrappstead
says that the Commission made the wrong decision, accepted the wrong evidence,
and breached his
Charter
rights.  Mr. Hrappstead disagrees with Cst.
Ng’s evidence and asserts that the Commission should have preferred his
evidence over that of Cst. Ng.

[
31
]

The Commission says that the defamation and
fraud claims are statute barred by the provisions of the
Limitation Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266.  The cause of action, if Mr. Hrappstead had one, would
run from the date when the alleged breach occurred, that is, the date of the
decision, April 7, 1999.

[
32
]

The Commission relies on s. 170 of the
Act
,
which grants immunity to the Commission and any of its members, officers,
servants, or agents from judicial review or any other proceedings for any act
done in the performance or intended performance of any duty, or the exercise or
the intended exercise of any power. Mr. Hrappstead cannot advance any claim
against the Commission, the panel members that rendered the decision, and any agent
of the Commission including officers that participated in the investigation on
behalf of the Commission, by virtue of that section.

[
33
]

The Commission argues that the counterclaim
should be dismissed under R. 19(24) on the basis that it is “...plain and obvious
that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action”:
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th)
266 at para.
34
.  The Commission says that Mr. Hrappstead’s evidence claims are
the proper subject of an appeal, which he did not file.  The
Charter

claims do not allege or disclose any infringement or violation of any of Mr.
Hrappstead’s
Charter
rights.  The Commission asserts that Mr. Hrappstead
has not pleaded sufficient facts to sustain the defamation or fraud claims.

[
34
]

The Commission further asserts that the claim is
unnecessary and vexatious because it does not disclose any cause of action
known to law.  The pleadings are frivolous because the claim is obviously
unsustainable.  The Commission asserts that the counterclaim is irrelevant and
embarrassing and that the pleadings are confusing.

[
35
]

The Commission argues that the counterclaim is
an abuse of process and a collateral attack.  There is a statutory appeal
process under the
Act
that must be followed.  Mr. Hrappstead cannot
commence other pleadings to attack the decision of the Commission, as that is a
collateral attack, which is improper:
Stephen v. HMTQ
,
2008 BCSC 1656
.

[
36
]

The Federal defendants by counterclaim adopt the
submission of the Commission in respect of R. 19(24).  They take no position on
the Commission’s R. 18A application.

[
37
]

The Provincial defendants by counterclaim also
adopt the submission made by the Commission on R. 19(24).  They take no
position in respect of the Commission’s application under RR. 18 or 18A.  The
Provincial defendants by counterclaim say that there are no specific
allegations against them in the pleadings, which is a radical defect in the
claim:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980.  The
Provincial defendants by counterclaim also assert that any claim against them
is statute barred in accordance with the
Limitation Act
.

[
38
]

Mr. Hrappstead makes the same argument in
respect of the assertions of the defendants by counterclaim in this context as
he does in respect of the Commission’s application for judgment under RR. 18
and/or 18A.

Decision

[
39
]

Rule 19(24) reads:

(24) At any stage of a proceeding the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim
or defence as the case may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
40
]

I find that it is plain and obvious that Mr. Hrappstead’s
statement of defence and counterclaim disclose no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt.

The defendant’s claims against all the defendants by counterclaim cannot
succeed.  Mr. Hrappstead feels that he did not receive a fair and impartial
hearing.  That is the proper subject of an appeal, which Mr. Hrappstead has not
taken from the Commission’s decision.  His evidence claims were dealt with in
the decision and any complaints in that regard are also the proper subject of
an appeal.  The
Charter
claims, the defamation claims, the investigation
claims, and the fraud claim do not disclose reasonable causes of action.  They
must therefore be struck under R. 19(24)(a).

[
41
]

I also agree with the plaintiff and the
defendants by counterclaim that the counterclaim is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous, and vexatious because it does not establish a cause of action or a
claim known to law.  The claims are statute barred in accordance with the
limitation periods defined in the
Limitation Act
.  Further, the
Commission and its panel members and its agents, officers, and employees are
protected from the defendant’s claims by s. 170 of the
Securities Act
.

[
42
]

I also find that the counterclaim is an abuse of
process and a collateral attack on the decision.  Mr. Hrappstead is attacking a
decision issued by the Ministry of Tribunal.  There are established routes for
appeal from those decisions.

[
43
]

As a result, the Hrappstead’s counterclaim does
not contain any
bona fide
triable issues and is therefore dismissed.

Costs

[
44
]

The parties did not address costs and may do so
by written submission.

“Gropper
J.”
